newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian vice president rekindles crisis.
newsitem.headline: Colombian vice president rekindles crisis.

text.p: Colombia's vice president has rekindled the country's political crisis by demanding that President Ernesto Samper resign, saying his inept leadership is driving the country to destruction.

But Samper, whose government has been severely weakened by a long-running scandal over his alleged ties to drug lords, responded to Thursday's dramatic request from Vice President Humberto de la Calle by saying he has no intention of stepping down and "leaving the country adrift."

The thick-skinned Samper, who has endured repeated calls for his resignation, also said that it was De la Calle who should leave office if he continued to insist on airing his differences with the government in public.

De la Calle, who resigned as Colombia's ambassador to Spain in July and returned from a Florida vacation on Thursday, said in an open letter to Samper read at a news conference that the government had lost all credibility because of charges Samper used millions of dollars in drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign.

He added that a de facto power vacuum had led to a situation in which Colombia appeared to be "falling to pieces" in the face of spiraling violence in the countryside and a sharp economic slowdown that has led to "talk not just of a recession but of a collapse."

"I believe that it is your inescapable duty as head of state to consider the certain and real possibility of resigning," De la Calle said in his letter. "This would allow for the formation of a government of national unity capable of leading the country on the crusade needed to salvage Colombia."

He added that a recent surge in leftist guerrilla activity added to the urgency of Samper's resignation, since he had failed as the country's commander-in-chief to confront what he described as an unprecedented threat to Colombia's "democratic stability."
"The government you preside over is at its worst hour in terms of credibility, legitimacy and capacity to act," De la Calle said.

Interior Minister Horacio Serpa told a news conference Thursday night that despite De la Calle's claim to the contrary Samper was firmly in charge of the ship of State and would ultimately guide it to "a safe port."
Even Serpa, Samper's right-hand man, was unable to deny that the widely perceived weakeness of the central government is being taken advantage of.

The government has faced a peasant revolt against its drug crop eradication program since mid-July. The revolt spread this week from three southern provinces to Norte de Santander in the country's north.

And scores of soldiers and police have been killed since Friday of last week in one of the worst offensives by leftist rebels in recent memory. As De la Calle noted in his letter, 60 soliders are being held as "prisoners of war" as a result of the offensive, and for the first time in more than three decades of guerrilla war the Colombian military appears to have lost all initiative.

There have been mixed reactions to De la Calle's call for Samper's resignation, with many people noting that he was elected on the same ticket as the president and with the same dubious source of financing. His remarks about the economy in particular were considered exaggerated by some, since the government has scaled back its economic growth forecast from an initial 4.9 percent but still predicts growth of 3.5 percent this year.

Few Colombians in or outside the government have taken issue, however, with the vice president's claim that more than one crisis and "disaster scenario" threatens "the democratic and social viability of our nation."
